clusters.canonical_name: AV Static/Dynamic Detection Engine Bypass Lifecycle
clusters.rationale: Singleton convergence note documenting the shared static-vs-dynamic detection engine decomposition across SEC670 and MalDev Academy.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 and MalDev Academy converge on the same lifecycle decomposition of AV detection
engines: static engines (signature/YARA-based, bypassable by changing the code base via
encoding, encryption, or metamorphism) versus dynamic engines (sandboxed execution,
bypassable by delaying execution, encrypting payloads, or triggering environment-gated
behavior). The vault's T-016 (NTAPI Hook Evasion) and T-020 (Anti-Analysis) implicitly
target these two layers but do not explicitly frame the dual-engine model as a
prerequisite concept. Documenting the lifecycle enables operators to map each evasion
primitive to the specific engine stage it defeats, producing a decision tree rather than
a flat technique list.
clusters.technical_anchor: Static signature engine (YARA rule matching) vs. dynamic sandbox execution engine — bypassed by code-base mutation vs. execution delay/encryption respectively
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton, conceptual framing rather than a new technique; overlaps existing T-016 and T-020 scope.

clusters.canonical_name: Win32 Enumeration API Taxonomy and Primitive Selection
clusters.rationale: Four notes from three atlas batches all describe the same gap: the vault lacks a dedicated enumeration-primitives card covering the Win32 API taxonomy and its tradeoffs.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 systematically compares CreateToolhelp32Snapshot (Process32First/Next, rich
metadata via PROCESSENTRY32), EnumProcesses (PID-only array, simplest), and
WTSEnumerateProcessesEx (session-aware, WTSEnumerateProcessesEx level info class) as
process-enumeration primitives with explicit tradeoffs: metadata depth vs. simplicity
vs. EDR visibility. The vault's T-004 (PEB Walker) deliberately avoids all three Win32
patterns, walking the PEB via gs:[0x60] → Ldr → InLoadOrderModuleList instead. A dedicated
card should document the full taxonomy across processes, users, groups, services,
scheduled tasks (ITaskScheduler COM), and network interfaces, with each primitive's
detection surface and the PEB-walker alternative positioned as the evasion path. The
cross-source convergence between SEC670 and MalDev Academy on this taxonomy elevates
its priority as a foundational discovery card.
clusters.technical_anchor: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot + Process32First/Next (PROCESSENTRY32W) vs. EnumProcesses (DWORD PID array) vs. WTSEnumerateProcessesEx — PEB walker via gs:[0x60] → PEB → Ldr → InLoadOrderModuleList as evasion alternative
clusters.priority_reason: Four member notes from three atlas batches; fills a critical foundational gap; cross-source convergence between SEC670 and MalDev Academy.

clusters.canonical_name: NtQuerySystemInformation as EDR-Resistant Enumeration Path
clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note about using the undocumented NT direct path for process enumeration to reduce EDR visibility.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 explicitly classifies NtQuerySystemInformation (with
SystemProcessInformation, class 5) as an 'undocumented' enumeration primitive alongside
the Win32 EnumProcesses and WTSEnumerateProcessesEx wrappers, signaling reduced EDR
visibility for direct NT API usage. The NT path returns a linked list of
SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION structures — each containing ProcessName, NumberOfThreads,
ThreadListHead, and HandleCount — without invoking the userland hooks that wrap the
Win32 equivalents. This positions NtQuerySystemInformation as an EDR-resistant
enumeration path distinct from both the PEB walker (T-004, self-only) and the Win32
taxonomy (T-023, system-wide but hooked). The vault should document the specific
information class, the linked-list traversal pattern (NextEntryOffset field), and the
detection-surface differential versus Win32 wrappers.
clusters.technical_anchor: NtQuerySystemInformation with SystemProcessInformation (class 5) — SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION structure with NextEntryOffset for linked-list traversal
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but names a specific NT direct technique with clear EDR-evasion value and a concrete information class.

clusters.canonical_name: Net* API Family as RPC-Derived Detection Surface
clusters.rationale: Singleton convergence note identifying the Net* API family and its underlying SAMRPC interfaces as a detection surface not currently addressed by the vault.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 covers NetUserEnum, NetGroupGetUsers, NetLocalGroupGetMembers, and NetUseEnum
as enumeration primitives that surface a detection surface the vault does not currently
address. These Net* APIs are thin wrappers over the SAMRPC interface — specifically the
Netr* RPC methods exposed by lsass.exe (e.g., NetrUserEnum, NetrGroupGetUsers,
NetrLocalGroupGetMembers via the samrpc pipe \PIPE\samr). EDRs that monitor RPC
dispatch at the lsass boundary can correlate these calls to reconnaissance activity,
making the Net* family operationally distinct from the Win32 process enumeration
primitives despite producing similar outputs. A card should document the API-to-RPC
mapping and the lsass.exe detection surface for each Net* function.
clusters.technical_anchor: NetUserEnum/NetGroupGetUsers/NetLocalGroupGetMembers → SAMRPC Netr* methods via  IPE\samr in lsass.exe
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but identifies a distinct detection surface (SAMRPC) not covered by existing cards; clear operational relevance for recon tradecraft.

clusters.canonical_name: Creative API Selection as Cross-Cutting Evasion Philosophy
clusters.rationale: Singleton convergence note articulating a cross-cutting philosophy — using less-common APIs to perform standard tasks in non-traditional ways — that underpins multiple existing T-NNN cards.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 units 39-40 articulate the philosophy that 'using less common APIs can bypass
EDR detection by performing standard tasks in non-traditional ways,' citing x86matthew
as a reference for creative API usage. This is not a single technique but a cross-cutting
design principle that underpins the vault's T-001 (RecycledGate, which reuses an existing
hooked function's syscall stub rather than fabricating one), T-004 (PEB Walker, which
resolves modules via PEB traversal instead of GetModuleHandle), T-014/T-016 (direct NT
API usage vs. Win32 wrappers), and T-022 (WinHTTP transport selection). A concept card
should frame this as a decision pattern: for each standard task (memory allocation,
process enumeration, module resolution, network transport), identify the canonical Win32
API, the less-common alternative, and the detection-surface differential.
clusters.technical_anchor: x86matthew creative API usage as reference — principle of performing standard tasks via non-traditional API paths to bypass EDR hooks
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but articulates a cross-cutting design philosophy that enriches five existing cards; high conceptual value.

clusters.canonical_name: Position-Independent C Shellcode Build Pipeline and Discipline
clusters.rationale: Four notes from three atlas batches all describe the same methodology: producing PIC shellcode from C with specific compiler settings and position-independence discipline.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 documents a complete methodology for producing position-independent shellcode
from C using Visual Studio compiler/linker settings: /GS- (no stack canary), /NODEFAULTLIB
(no CRT), /SUBSYSTEM:NATIVE, /NOENTRY (no default entry), custom entry point via
/ENTRY: flag, /SDL- (no security checks), and no C++ exceptions. The discipline requires
avoiding the heap (no malloc/new), avoiding external references (no imports resolved by
the loader), and avoiding the .data section (use stack-allocated constants or
runtime-resolved strings). Compiler intrinsics (__readgsqword, __readmsr) replace their
CRT-wrapped equivalents. The vault's T-020 (Anti-Analysis) and T-021 (Crypto &
Obfuscation) cover shellcode encoding formats (IPv4/IPv6/MAC/UUID/words) but do not
document the build pipeline that produces the raw shellcode bytes in the first place.
This card should be the prerequisite reference for all shellcode-emitting techniques.
clusters.technical_anchor: Visual Studio linker flags /GS- /NODEFAULTLIB /SUBSYSTEM:NATIVE /NOENTRY /ENTRY:ShellcodeBegin /SDL- — gs:[0x60] PEB access via __readgsqword intrinsic
clusters.priority_reason: Four member notes from three atlas batches; fills a critical prerequisite gap for all shellcode-producing techniques.

clusters.canonical_name: Thread Creation Internals (NtCreateThreadEx / PspCreateThread)
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note identifying the kernel-side thread creation path as a prerequisite concept for all thread-based injection techniques.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 unit 10 explains the kernel-side thread creation path that all thread-based
injection techniques ultimately invoke: NtCreateThreadEx → PspCreateThread, including
parameter-to-flag conversion, Client ID and TEB insertion into an attribute list, and
the local vs. remote dispatch fork (PspCreateThread for current process vs. remote
process via the ThreadContext parameter). The vault's T-007 (NtCreateThreadEx Remote
Thread), T-008 (Thread Hijacking), T-012 (APC Injection), and T-013 (Shellcode Runner)
all terminate at this path but do not document the kernel internals as a shared
prerequisite. A concept card should map the CreateThread → NtCreateThreadEx →
PspCreateThread dispatch chain, the ETHREAD/InitialTeb fields populated, and how each
injection technique (remote thread, APC, thread hijack) diverges at the point of
thread-context construction.
clusters.technical_anchor: NtCreateThreadEx → PspCreateThread — Client ID and TEB insertion into thread attribute list; local vs. remote dispatch via ThreadContext parameter
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents a kernel internals prerequisite shared by four existing injection cards.

clusters.canonical_name: IFEO GlobalFlag + SilentProcessExit Persistence
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note for a registry-driven persistence mechanism triggered on target process exit, not currently in T-017.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 documents IFEO (Image File Execution Options) GlobalFlag set to value 512
(FLG_ENABLE_SYSTEM_DISABLE_KEY) combined with SilentProcessExit registry settings —
specifically ReportingMode and MonitorProcess under
HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit — as a registry-driven
persistence mechanism triggered when the target process exits. The Windows Error
Reporting service (WerFault.exe) reads these keys and launches the MonitorProcess
executable on target exit, providing an event-driven persistence trigger distinct from
boot-time or logon-time mechanisms. T-017 (Five-Layer Persistence) covers COM hijack,
NTFS EA, schtask, TLS callback, and PhantomPersist but does not include IFEO +
SilentProcessExit. The mechanism is particularly valuable because it executes under
WER's privilege context and triggers on an abnormal exit event, blending with legitimate
crash-reporting telemetry.
clusters.technical_anchor: IFEO GlobalFlag = 512 (FLG_ENABLE_SYSTEM_DISABLE_KEY) + SilentProcessExit ReportingMode/MonitorProcess under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit — WerFault.exe launches MonitorProcess on target exit
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents a distinct persistence entry point not in T-017; event-driven trigger adds operational value.

clusters.canonical_name: Port Monitor DLL Persistence via AddMonitor
clusters.rationale: Two coverage-gap notes from different atlas batches describe the same AddMonitor-based persistence mechanism absent from T-017.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 covers abusing the AddMonitor API (winspool.drv) to register a custom DLL as a
port monitor for persistence via the print spooler service (spoolsv.exe). The registered
DLL is loaded by spoolsv.exe at service startup, executing in SYSTEM privilege context.
The monitor entry persists in the registry under
HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors with the DLL path, and the spooler
service loads it on every restart. T-017's persistence suite (COM hijack, NTFS EA,
schtask, TLS callback, PhantomPersist) does not include this mechanism. Port monitor
persistence is distinct because it executes under the print spooler's SYSTEM context,
triggers on service start rather than user logon, and blends with legitimate printer
driver installation activity. The AddMonitor call itself is a privileged operation
requiring SeLoadDriverPrivilege.
clusters.technical_anchor: AddMonitor API (winspool.drv) registering DLL under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control rint\Monitors — loaded by spoolsv.exe at SYSTEM privilege
clusters.priority_reason: Two member notes from different batches; documents a SYSTEM-privilege persistence mechanism absent from T-017.

clusters.canonical_name: AppInit_DLLs Persistence and DLL Injection
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note for AppInit_DLLs as a DLL injection and persistence mechanism not in T-017.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670's InitToWinInit lab covers AppInit_DLLs as a DLL injection and persistence
mechanism where any DLL path listed in the registry value
HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\AppInit_DLLs is loaded into
every process that loads user32.dll. The machine-wide RequireSignedAppInit_DLLs value
controls whether only signed DLLs are loaded (set to 1 on modern Windows). T-017 does
not include this technique. The mechanism is particularly relevant for its broad
injection surface — affecting all user32.dll-loading processes — but is diminishing in
effectiveness due to the signing requirement on Windows 10+ and the introduction of
AppInit_DLLs exclusions for certain system processes. A card should document the
registry path, the RequireSignedAppInit_DLLs gate, the user32.dll load-order dependency,
and the diminishing operational window on modern Windows.
clusters.technical_anchor: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\AppInit_DLLs (semicolon-delimited DLL paths) + RequireSignedAppInit_DLLs gate — injected into all user32.dll-loading processes
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents a classic persistence/DLL-injection mechanism absent from T-017; diminishing but still operational.

clusters.canonical_name: Reflective DLL Injection and Manual PE Mapping
clusters.rationale: Singleton convergence note on reflective DLL loading as a technique covered across multiple SEC670 units and converging with the vault's T-013.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 dedicates multiple units (35-40) to Reflective DLL Injection, covering Stephen
Fewer's original technique and the manual mapping process: CreateFileA to read the DLL
from disk, ReadFile into a buffer, VirtualAlloc with PAGE_READWRITE for the mapped image,
PE header parsing (IMAGE_DOS_HEADER → IMAGE_NT_HEADERS → SectionHeader array), section
relocations (relocation table traversal via IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_BASERELOC), import
resolution (IAT via IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT → LoadLibrary/GetProcAddress), and
final DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH call to DllMain. The vault's T-013 (Shellcode Runner) covers
shellcode execution but not the full reflective DLL loading pipeline. The cross-source
convergence elevates this as a well-documented mainstream technique that should be
represented as a dedicated card distinct from simple shellcode execution, covering the
PE mapping sequence, relocation table processing, and IAT resolution as distinct phases.
clusters.technical_anchor: Stephen Fewer reflective loading — VirtualAlloc + IMAGE_DOS_HEADER.e_lfanew → IMAGE_NT_HEADERS → SectionHeader relocations via IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_BASERELOC + IAT via IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT → DllMain(DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but covers a named mainstream technique (Stephen Fewer) across 6 SEC670 units; fills a gap adjacent to T-013.

clusters.canonical_name: GUI Syscall Surface via win32u.dll / win32k.sys
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note identifying a distinct syscall dispatch path (win32u.dll → win32k.sys) not documented in the vault's syscall suite.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 units 30-31 distinguish native syscalls (ntdll.dll → kernel/executive via the
syscall instruction) from GUI syscalls (win32u.dll → win32k.sys via the same syscall
instruction but a different dispatch table). Examples include NtUserOpenClipboard,
NtUserCloseClipboard, NtUserGetMessage, NtUserFindWindowEx, and NtUserSetWindowsHookEx
— all routed through win32u.dll rather than ntdll.dll. The vault's syscall dispatch
suite (T-001 through T-006) documents only the native ntdll path. The GUI syscall path
is operationally distinct because win32k.sys has its own syscall table (a separate
region of the SSDT), its own SSN numbering, and its own hook surface — EDRs that
instrument only ntdll stubs miss GUI syscalls entirely. A card should document the
win32u.dll stub structure, the win32k.sys SSDT region, SSN resolution for GUI functions,
and the detection-surface differential versus native syscalls.
clusters.technical_anchor: win32u.dll syscall stubs → win32k.sys SSDT — NtUserOpenClipboard/NtUserCloseClipboard/NtUserGetMessage dispatched via separate GUI syscall table, not ntdll
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but identifies a novel syscall dispatch path with distinct detection surface; S-tier for novelty and operational value.

clusters.canonical_name: KUSER_SHARED_DATA Syscall Dispatch Flag in Stub Replication
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note about the KUSER_SHARED_DATA flag at 0x7FFE0308 that every ntdll syscall stub checks, relevant to stub fabrication techniques.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 unit 32 documents the 'test byte ptr [7FFE0308h],1' check inside every ntdll
syscall stub, which selects between the 'syscall' instruction (modern path) and legacy
'int 2Eh' dispatch. The byte at 0x7FFE0308 is within the KUSER_SHARED_DATA structure
(SystemCallPad field at offset 0x308). Techniques that fabricate or copy syscall stubs
(T-001 RecycledGate, T-006 Picusstons) must replicate this check correctly or risk
dispatching via the legacy interrupt path on systems where the flag is clear. The vault's
stub implementations use hardcoded 'mov eax, SSN; syscall' sequences that omit this
check. A card should document the KUSER_SHARED_DATA layout (shared at 0x7FFE0000,
user-mode mapped), the specific offset 0x308, the flag semantics, and the implications
for stub fabrication — including whether the omission produces detectable anomalies.
clusters.technical_anchor: KUSER_SHARED_DATA at 0x7FFE0000 — SystemCallPad byte at offset 0x308 ('test byte ptr [7FFE0308h],1') in ntdll syscall stubs selecting syscall vs. int 2Eh dispatch
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents a specific KUSER_SHARED_DATA field that affects stub fabrication correctness across T-001 and T-006.

clusters.canonical_name: Foundational Syscall Mechanics (Stub Structure, SSN Variance, Routing)
clusters.rationale: Singleton convergence note identifying the shared syscall-stub foundation (stub structure, SSN variance, native-vs-GUI routing) that motivates the entire vault syscall suite.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 units 24-34 cover the syscall stub structure (mov eax, SSN; test byte ptr
[7FFE0308h],1; syscall; ret), SSN version-variance across Windows builds (SSNs are
unstable across versions but stable within a build), and the native-vs-GUI routing
that motivates the entire HUGIN syscall-dispatch suite (T-001 through T-006). The
convergence across SEC670, MalDev Academy, and the vault's own implementation confirms
these as foundational prerequisites. A concept card should document the stub byte
sequence, the SSN assignment pattern (Nt* functions assigned sequential SSNs in
alphabetical order within each build), the SSN-without-hardcoding approaches (hell's
gate, halos gate, tartarus gate), and the relationship between direct syscall dispatch
and EDR hook evasion. This card would serve as the navigation hub for T-001 through
T-006.
clusters.technical_anchor: ntdll syscall stub byte pattern: mov eax, SSN (4-byte immediate) + 'test byte ptr [7FFE0308h],1' + syscall + ret — SSNs assigned alphabetically per build
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents the foundational prerequisite for the entire syscall suite (T-001-T-006); high navigational value.

clusters.canonical_name: IAT and Inline Hooking as EDR Userland Mechanisms
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note about the two primary userland hooking mechanisms EDRs employ, which T-016 evades but does not document as background.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 units 35-40 document the two primary userland hooking mechanisms EDRs employ:
IAT pointer overwrite (flipping the IAT entry's memory protection to PAGE_READWRITE via
VirtualProtect, replacing the function pointer with a detour, restoring protection) and
inline prologue patching (overwriting the first 5-7 bytes of the function prologue with
a jmp to the detour, saving the original bytes for pass-through). The vault's T-016
(NTAPI Hook Evasion) evades these hooks by using direct syscalls but does not document
the hook mechanisms themselves as background. A prerequisite card should describe both
hook types, the VirtualProtect-based IAT flip, the inline prologue patch with trampoline
construction, the saved-byte restoration pattern, and how each hook type is detected
(scanning IAT for non-module-range pointers; scanning prologue for jmp opcodes). This
background makes T-016's evasion approach comprehensible to readers without prior EDR
internals knowledge.
clusters.technical_anchor: IAT hook: VirtualProtect PAGE_READWRITE → overwrite function pointer → restore protection; Inline hook: prologue byte patch with jmp rel32 (0xE8/E9) + trampoline with saved original bytes
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents the EDR hook mechanisms that T-016 evades; high prerequisite value for understanding T-016.

clusters.canonical_name: SysWhispers3 Syscall Stub Code Generation
clusters.rationale: Singleton convergence note comparing SysWhispers3 as the standard external stub-generation tool against the vault's hand-rolled stubs.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 units 15-16 cover SysWhispers3 as the standard external tool for generating
syscall stubs, including the egg-hunter variant (searching ntdll memory for a known
byte pattern to locate a legitimate stub) and the random-jump variant (jumping into
the middle of a legitimate stub to avoid prologue-based detection). The vault implements
its own stubs (T-001 RecycledGate, which borrows a hooked function's stub; T-006
Picusstons, hand-rolled PIC stubs) rather than using SysWhispers3. A card should
document SysWhispers3's code-generation model (Python templates producing C/H files
with stub definitions), the egg-hunter pattern (scanning for {4C 8B D1 B8 ... 00 00 07
00} byte signature in ntdll), the random-jump approach (jumping to offset N within a
legitimate stub), and how these compare to the vault's T-001 and T-006 approaches in
terms of detection surface and maintainability.
clusters.technical_anchor: SysWhispers3 egg-hunter: scan ntdll for byte signature {4C 8B D1 B8 ?? ?? ?? 00 F6 04 25 08 03 FE 7F 01 75 03 0F 05 C3} — random-jump: JMP to offset within legitimate stub
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents the standard external tooling (SysWhispers3) against which the vault's hand-rolled stubs should be compared.

clusters.canonical_name: WinINet vs WinHTTP for C2 Transport
clusters.rationale: Two notes from different atlas batches (one gap, one convergence) both identify the WinINet API family as an alternative C2 transport not documented in T-022.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 documents InternetConnect + HttpOpenRequest (WinINet, wininet.dll) as the
canonical HTTP C2 session API sequence, covering InternetOpen (session handle),
InternetConnect (server handle with port), HttpOpenRequest (request handle with method
and path), HttpSendRequest (transmit), and InternetReadFile (response body). The vault's
T-022 networking suite currently lists WinHTTP-based download (winhttp_dl.rs using
WinHttpOpen/WinHttpConnect/WinHttpOpenRequest/WinHttpSendRequest) as the staged download
mechanism. WinINet and WinHTTP are distinct API families: WinINet (wininet.dll) is the
higher-level API with built-in IE cache, cookie, and proxy support, historically used
by web browsers; WinHTTP (winhttp.dll) is the lighter API designed for server-side and
non-interactive HTTP. A card should document both API sequences side-by-side, the
detection-surface differential (WinINet hooks are common in EDRs; WinHTTP hooks less
so but increasing), and the operational tradeoffs (cache artifacts vs. stealth, cookie
persistence vs. statelessness, proxy behavior).
clusters.technical_anchor: WinINet: InternetOpen → InternetConnect → HttpOpenRequest → HttpSendRequest → InternetReadFile (wininet.dll) vs. WinHTTP: WinHttpOpen → WinHttpConnect → WinHttpOpenRequest → WinHttpSendRequest → WinHttpReadData (winhttp.dll)
clusters.priority_reason: Two member notes from different batches; documents an alternative C2 transport API family with distinct detection surface.

clusters.canonical_name: Socket-Handle Reverse Shell via STARTUPINFO Inheritance
clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note about the classic reverse-shell construction via STARTUPINFO handle inheritance.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 units 25-26 cover the classic reverse-shell construction where a socket handle
(WSASocket/WSAStartup) is placed in STARTUPINFO's hStdInput, hStdOutput, and hStdError
fields (STARTF_USESTDHANDLES flag in dwFlags), and cmd.exe is spawned with CreateProcessA
using the inherited handle table. This redirects the child process's stdin/stdout/stderr
to the network socket, producing an interactive shell over TCP without allocating a
console window (CREATE_NO_WINDOW flag). The vault's T-022 (networking) and T-023 (not
present — gap) do not document this construction. The technique is foundational for
client-side post-exploitation and is the basis for more elaborate shells (e.g., named
pipe relay, PTY emulation). A card should document the STARTUPINFO field layout, the
handle-inheritance requirement (bInheritHandles = TRUE in SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES), the
CREATE_NO_WINDOW / STARTF_USESTDHANDLES flag combination, and the detection surface
(CreateProcess with cmd.exe + socket handle is a well-known IoC).
clusters.technical_anchor: STARTUPINFO.hStdInput/hStdOutput/hStdError = socket handle (WSASocket) + dwFlags STARTF_USESTDHANDLES + CreateProcessA(cmd.exe, bInheritHandles=TRUE, CREATE_NO_WINDOW)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents a classic reverse-shell primitive foundational to client-side post-exploitation.

clusters.canonical_name: C2 Check-in Loop with Jittered Sleep and JSON Tasking
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note about the implant check-in loop and JSON tasking protocol, which T-022 does not document.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 units 12-14 document the implant check-in loop (while/try/catch/sleep with
jittered interval) and the JSON tasking protocol: UUID-based task IDs, CheckTasks
request parsing, RunTask execution dispatch, and result reporting back to the C2. The
jitter pattern adds ±N% randomness to the base sleep interval to defeat beacon-
timing analysis. The vault's T-022 documents HTTP transport (WinHTTP-based download)
but does not document the tasking loop, the jitter algorithm, or the JSON protocol
structure. A card should document the check-in state machine (initial check-in → task
poll → task execute → result report → sleep(jitter) → repeat), the jitter calculation
(base_interval * (1 ± random(0, jitter_pct))), the JSON schema for task requests and
responses, and the relationship to T-005 (Sleep Obfuscation), which must integrate with
the jittered sleep interval.
clusters.technical_anchor: Check-in loop: while(true) { CheckTasks(UUID) → RunTask → ReportResult → Sleep(base_interval ± jitter_pct) } — JSON task schema with UUID task IDs
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents the C2 tasking loop and jitter algorithm that integrates T-022 transport with T-005 sleep obfuscation.

clusters.canonical_name: CNG (BCrypt*) over Legacy CryptoAPI (Crypt*) Migration
clusters.rationale: Three convergence notes from three atlas batches all recommend CNG BCrypt* APIs over legacy CryptoAPI Crypt* functions for shellcode encryption.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 explicitly frames the deprecated Crypt* family (CryptAcquireContextA with
PROV_RSA_AES, CryptDeriveKey, CryptEncrypt) versus the recommended CNG BCrypt* family
(bcrypt.h: BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider, BCryptSetProperty, BCryptGenerateSymmetricKey,
BCryptEncrypt) as a tradecraft decision. CNG is positioned as 'more advanced and
extensible' than CryptoAPI, with support for authenticated encryption modes (GCM,
CCM) that the legacy API lacks. The vault's T-021 uses Rust's aes-gcm crate rather
than either Windows API family, which is appropriate for the Rust-based dark_crystal
crate but leaves CNG and CryptoAPI paths undocumented for operators working in C/C++.
A card should document the CNG API sequence for AES-GCM (BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider
with BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM → BCryptSetProperty with BCRYPT_CHAINING_MODE_GCM →
BCryptGenerateSymmetricKey → BCryptEncrypt with BCRYPT_AUTHENTICATED_CIPHER_MODE_INFO),
the deprecation timeline of CryptoAPI, and the operational tradeoff versus using a
language-native crypto crate.
clusters.technical_anchor: CNG AES-GCM: BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider(BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM) → BCryptSetProperty(BCRYPT_CHAINING_MODE, BCRYPT_CHAIN_MODE_GCM) → BCryptGenerateSymmetricKey → BCryptEncrypt with BCRYPT_AUTHENTICATED_CIPHER_MODE_INFO — vs. deprecated CryptAcquireContextA(PROV_RSA_AES)
clusters.priority_reason: Three member notes from three atlas batches; cross-source convergence on CNG as the recommended Windows-native crypto API.

clusters.canonical_name: XOR with Key — Encoding or Encryption Classification
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note about the classification debate for XOR-with-key, which the vault's T-021 treats as encoding.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 surfaces the long-standing debate over whether XOR with a key constitutes
encoding or encryption, noting that the presence of a key supports the encryption
classification. The vault's T-021 treats shellcode encoding formats (IPv4/IPv6/MAC/
UUID/words) as encoding — which is correct for format-only transforms — but does not
address the XOR-with-key semantic boundary. The distinction matters operationally
because some EDR/AV vendors classify XOR-with-key as encryption (triggering
entropy-based detection) while others classify it as encoding (triggering no
detection). A concept card should document the XOR operation (plaintext[i] ^ key[i %
key_len]), the entropy profile of XOR output (preserves byte-frequency distribution of
the key, not the plaintext), the detection differential (high-entropy keys produce
high-entropy output detectable by Shannon entropy analysis), and the classification
rationale (presence of a key → encryption; absence of a key → encoding).
clusters.technical_anchor: XOR operation: plaintext[i] ^ key[i % key_len] — Shannon entropy of output depends on key entropy, not plaintext entropy; presence of key → encryption classification per some EDR vendors
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton, conceptual classification debate rather than a new technique; limited operational impact.

clusters.canonical_name: Windows Data Type System as Architecture Portability Rationale
clusters.rationale: Singleton concept note about the Windows data type system (DWORD, BOOL, BOOLEAN) as an architecture-insulation layer; concept node, not a technique.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 explains that Windows data types (DWORD, BOOL, BOOLEAN, HANDLE, LPVOID) were
created to insulate source code from 16-bit to 32-bit to 64-bit architecture
transitions. BOOL is a 32-bit int (typedef int BOOL), BOOLEAN is a BYTE (typedef
unsigned char BOOLEAN), DWORD is a 32-bit unsigned long (typedef unsigned long DWORD),
and HANDLE is a void* (sizeof varies by architecture). This matters for FFI bindings
(Rust extern "C", Go cgo) where using the wrong native type produces ABI mismatches
that are silent on one architecture but corrupt data on another. A concept card should
document the type hierarchy (Win32 typedefs → C base types → actual sizes by
architecture), the BOOL vs BOOLEAN distinction (4 bytes vs 1 byte — a common source
of FFI bugs), the pointer-size types (HANDLE, LPVOID, PSTR), and how the vault's Rust
bindings map these types (e.g., BOOL → i32, HANDLE → isize, DWORD → u32).
clusters.technical_anchor: BOOL = typedef int (4 bytes, i32 in Rust) vs BOOLEAN = typedef unsigned char (1 byte, u8 in Rust) vs DWORD = typedef unsigned long (4 bytes, u32) vs HANDLE = void* (pointer-sized, isize)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton concept node; educational completeness value, no direct operational impact.

clusters.canonical_name: Certutil as Base64 LOLBin for Shellcode Transformation
clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note about certutil.exe -encode as a native OS utility for Base64-transforming shellcode.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 references certutil.exe -encode (and -decode) as a native OS utility for
Base64-transforming shellcode, alongside the API-based CryptStringToBinaryA (decode) and
CryptBinaryToStringA (encode) approach. The vault's T-020 (Anti-Analysis) covers
KnownDlls and parent-process checks but does not document LOLBin (Living Off the Land
Binary) usage for shellcode transformation. certutil.exe is a signed Microsoft binary
that can decode Base64 files to binary, making it useful for writing raw shellcode to
disk without introducing custom tooling. The command 'certutil -decode input.b64
output.bin' produces the raw binary from a Base64-encoded input file. A card should
document the certutil -encode/-decode syntax, the CryptStringToBinaryA/
CryptBinaryToStringA API equivalents (CRYPT_STRING_BASE64 flag), the detection surface
(certutil with -decode is a well-known LOLBin IoC), and the operational tradeoff
(signed-binary stealth vs. behavioral detection).
clusters.technical_anchor: certutil.exe -decode <input.b64> <output.bin> (Base64 → binary) + CryptStringToBinaryA with CRYPT_STRING_BASE64 flag (API equivalent)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents a named LOLBin (certutil) with a concrete command and API equivalent; operational tradecraft value.

clusters.canonical_name: SAL Annotations (_In_, _Out_, _Inout_) for Win32 API Bindings
clusters.rationale: Singleton concept note about SAL annotations as a compiler-checked safety mechanism for Win32 API usage; concept node.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SANS SEC670 emphasizes SAL annotations (_In_, _Out_, _Inout_, _In_opt_, _Out_opt_,
_In_reads_, _Out_writes_) as a compiler-checked safety mechanism for Win32 API usage
and notes that most online documentation omits them, requiring direct header inspection
(windows.h, winternl.h, ntifs.h). The vault's syscall stubs (T-001, T-004) and FFI
bindings do not currently include SAL annotations in their function signatures. A
concept card should document the SAL annotation hierarchy (directional: _In_/_Out_/
_Inout_; optional: _opt_ suffix; buffer-size: _In_reads_(n)/_Out_writes_(n); pointer
validity: _Maybenull_), how the /analyze compiler flag enables static SAL checking,
and the specific annotations for the NT functions the vault uses
(e.g., NtQuerySystemInformation is _In_ SYSTEM_INFORMATION_CLASS, _Inout_ PVOID, _In_
ULONG, _Out_opt_ PULONG). This improves the correctness of FFI bindings in Rust and
C/C++ alike.
clusters.technical_anchor: SAL annotations: _In_ (input, must be valid), _Out_ (output, must be writable), _Inout_ (both), _In_reads_(n) (buffer of n elements), _opt_ suffix (optional/can be NULL) — enforced by /analyze compiler flag
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton concept node; educational/completeness value, no direct operational impact.

clusters.canonical_name: Windows Calling Conventions for Syscall Stubs and FFI
clusters.rationale: Singleton concept note about Windows calling conventions (__stdcall, __cdecl, __fastcall, __thiscall) as a prerequisite for syscall stub and FFI implementation.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 dedicates an entire module to Windows calling conventions: __stdcall
(Win32 API default, callee cleans stack, arguments pushed right-to-left), __cdecl
(C runtime default, caller cleans stack, variadic-compatible), __fastcall
(first 2 args in ECX/EDX on x86, rest on stack; on x64 superseded by the unified
ABI), __thiscall (C++ member functions, this in ECX on x86). The x64 unified calling
convention (RCX/RDX/R8/R9 for first 4 integer args, XMM0-3 for floats, shadow space
allocation by caller) is the one that actually matters for the vault's syscall stubs
and NT API FFI on x64 Windows. The vault's T-001 through T-006 all assume this
convention but do not document it. A concept card should document each convention's
stack-cleanup responsibility, argument-passing registers, name mangling, and the
x64 unified ABI shadow space (32 bytes) — particularly relevant for hand-rolled
syscall stubs where the shadow space must be allocated or the return address
clobbers the first 8 bytes of where RCX was expected to persist.
clusters.technical_anchor: x64 unified ABI: RCX/RDX/R8/R9 for first 4 integer args, 32-byte shadow space (_RSP+0..0x20) allocated by caller, return value in RAX, stack 16-byte aligned pre-call
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton concept but foundational for understanding all syscall stub implementations (T-001-T-006); high prerequisite value.

clusters.canonical_name: Windows API Foundations — Create* Kernel Objects, Handles, SAL
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note about the foundational Windows API patterns (kernel objects, handles, SAL) that T-014/T-015/T-016 assume.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 Book 1 dedicates substantial material to SAL annotations, the Create* kernel-
object/handle pattern (CreateFile/CreateProcess/CreateThread/CreateEvent returning a
HANDLE with ref-count semantics), the CloseHandle/GetLastError error model, and the
WaitFor* synchronization family (WaitForSingleObject, WaitForMultipleObjects). The
vault's T-014 (Module Stomping), T-015 (not specified), and T-016 (NTAPI Hook Evasion)
all assume familiarity with these patterns but do not document them as a shared
prerequisite. A concept card should document the handle table model (per-process handle
table, handle value encoding with audit/inherit bits), the Create/Close lifecycle, the
GetLastError/HRESULT/NTSTATUS error-code regimes (and how they differ), and the
WaitFor* family's relationship to signaled/non-signaled kernel objects. This card
would serve as a navigation hub for readers new to Windows internals approaching the
vault's technique cards.
clusters.technical_anchor: Create* → HANDLE (per-process handle table with Entry containing Lock/Inheritable/Audit/Protect-from-close bits) + CloseHandle + GetLastError (Win32 error) vs HRESULT vs NTSTATUS (ntstatus.h) error regimes
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents foundational Windows API patterns assumed by three existing cards; high prerequisite value.

clusters.rationale: Singleton convergence note confirming the vault's Rust-based architecture aligns with cross-source endorsement of Rust for offensive tools.
clusters.consolidated_description:

on this same premise (dark_crystal and client_rust are Rust crates). The convergence

(zero-cost abstractions, memory safety without GC, extern "C" FFI for Win32/NT API
binding, #[no_std] for PIC shellcode, proc macros for compile-time payload
transformation), the tradeoffs versus C/C++ (compilation time, binary size, learning
curve), and the specific crates the vault uses (windows-sys for Win32 bindings,
aes-gcm for crypto).
clusters.technical_anchor: Rust extern "C" FFI for Win32/NT API binding + #[no_std] for PIC shellcode + windows-sys crate (raw FFI bindings) + aes-gcm crate
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton convergence; validates existing architecture choice rather than introducing a new technique.

clusters.canonical_name: PE Format Internals — MZ Header, DOS Stub, Section Layout
clusters.rationale: Two concept notes from different atlas batches both describe the PE file format structure as a foundational concept; concept node, not a technique.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 introduces the PE file format at a bird's-eye level — MZ header (IMAGE_DOS_HEADER),
DOS stub, e_lfanew offset (at 0x3C in IMAGE_DOS_HEADER) to IMAGE_NT_HEADERS, COFF file
header (IMAGE_FILE_HEADER), Optional Header (IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER), section headers
(IMAGE_SECTION_HEADER array), and image pages. The .text section holds executable code;
.rdata holds read-only data including the Export Directory (whose RVA is in
IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT of the DataDirectory array). This structural layout is
the foundation for module stomping (T-006, overwriting a loaded module's .text section),
function stomping (overwriting specific export function bytes), and reflective loading
(T-013, manual PE mapping). A concept card should document the field-by-field layout
of IMAGE_DOS_HEADER (e_magic 'MZ', e_lfanew at 0x3C), IMAGE_NT_HEADERS (Signature
'PE\0\0', FileHeader, OptionalHeader), the DataDirectory[16] array, and the section
header fields (VirtualAddress, SizeOfRawData, PointerToRawData, Characteristics).
clusters.technical_anchor: IMAGE_DOS_HEADER.e_lfanew at offset 0x3C → IMAGE_NT_HEADERS (Signature 'PE��' + IMAGE_FILE_HEADER + IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER) → DataDirectory[IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT] → IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY in .rdata
clusters.priority_reason: Two member notes from different batches; concept node but foundational prerequisite for module stomping, reflective loading, and PE manipulation.

clusters.canonical_name: .def File Ordinal-Based Export Control
clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note about .def files for ordinal-based export declaration, operationally distinct from name-based resolution.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 covers .def files as a way to declare DLL exports with explicit ordinals and
library/version metadata. The .def file syntax includes EXPORTS section with function
name, ordinal (@N suffix), NONAME attribute (export by ordinal only, hiding the name),
and PRIVATE attribute (not visible in the import library). Ordinal-based export
resolution is operationally distinct from name-based resolution: GetProcAddress(hModule,
MAKEINTRESOURCE(ordinal)) resolves by ordinal, which bypasses name-based EDR hooks on
GetProcAddress and produces no export-name string in the import table. The vault's
T-008 (Thread Hijacking) and T-016 (NTAPI Hook Evasion) could benefit from ordinal-based
resolution for stealthy function lookup. A card should document the .def file syntax,
the linker /DEF flag, the MAKEINTRESOURCE(ordinal) macro for GetProcAddress, the
NONAME/Private attributes, and the detection surface (ordinal-only exports are a known
DLL-cloaking IoC).
clusters.technical_anchor: .def file EXPORTS section: FunctionName @Ordinal NONAME PRIVATE — resolved via GetProcAddress(hModule, MAKEINTRESOURCE(ordinal)) bypassing name-based hooks
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents a distinct export-control mechanism with evasion implications; named technique with concrete .def syntax.

SEC670 Unit 39 explicitly references the UACMe project's FusionScanFiles routine,
identifying UACMe as the canonical UAC bypass research corpus. The vault's T-021 covers
UAC bypass via CMSTP (Microsoft Connection Manager Profile Installer) and slui.exe
(Windows Activation executable) registry manipulation. UACMe documents 80+ UAC bypass
methods organized by auto-elevation mechanism (ICMLuaUtil, IColorDataProxy,
IEditionUpgradeManager, IFwCplUser), each exploiting a different auto-elevated COM
interface or binary. A card should document the UACMe corpus structure, the auto-
elevation criteria (requestedExecutionLevel=RequireAdministrator in manifest +
autoElevate=true), the COM-interface-based bypass pattern (instantiating an
elevated COM object and calling its methods to execute arbitrary actions), and the
FusionScanFiles routine specifically (which uses IFileOperation via elevated COM to
copy/replace files in protected locations).
clusters.technical_anchor: UACMe FusionScanFiles: elevated COM interface IFileOperation (CLSID {3ad00546-1E8F-4C95-A33A-9C9B20BEE633}) via ICMLuaUtil::ShellExec — bypass via autoElevate=true manifest + CoCreateInstance with elevated token
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents a named corpus (UACMe) with 80+ methods and a specific routine (FusionScanFiles); privesc reference value.

clusters.canonical_name: Windows Service Architecture and Failure-Action Persistence
clusters.rationale: Two coverage-gap notes from different atlas batches both describe service-based persistence: the service architecture (main thread, service thread, control handler) and the failure-action resilience mechanism.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 documents the three-component Windows service architecture required to construct
a functional service: the main thread (calling StartServiceCtrlDispatcher with a
SERVICE_TABLE_ENTRY), the service thread (the actual ServiceMain callback), and the
control handler (registered via RegisterServiceCtrlHandler for
SERVICE_CONTROL_STOP/PAUSE/CONTINUE events). For persistence resilience, the
SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONS structure is set via ChangeServiceConfig2 with
SERVICE_CONFIG_FAILURE_ACTIONS, specifying SC_ACTION_RESTART with a delay (e.g., 60
seconds) — ensuring the service auto-restarts on failure and thus survives
termination. The vault's T-017 documents PhantomPersist with a 30-minute resilience
monitor but does not document the service architecture or the failure-action
mechanism. A card should document the service registration sequence (CreateService →
StartServiceCtrlDispatcher → RegisterServiceCtrlHandler → SetServiceStatus), the
ChangeServiceConfig2 failure-action API, and how the auto-restart creates a
self-healing persistence layer.
clusters.technical_anchor: StartServiceCtrlDispatcher(SERVICE_TABLE_ENTRY) → ServiceMain → RegisterServiceCtrlHandler + ChangeServiceConfig2(SERVICE_CONFIG_FAILURE_ACTIONS, SC_ACTION_RESTART with delay) for auto-restart resilience
clusters.priority_reason: Two member notes from different batches; documents a SYSTEM-privilege persistence mechanism with auto-restart resilience absent from T-017.

clusters.canonical_name: PE Export Directory Traversal for API Resolution
clusters.rationale: Two notes (one convergence, one emerging-tradecraft) both describe the PE export directory traversal as the shared foundation for T-004, T-006, and T-008 — the same mechanism reimplemented as custom GetProcAddress.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 units 23-32 walk through the PE export resolution chain: IMAGE_DOS_HEADER →
e_lfanew → IMAGE_NT_HEADERS → OptionalHeader.DataDirectory[IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT]
→ IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY (in .rdata) → AddressOfNames (DWORD RVA array of name
pointers) → AddressOfNameOrdinals (WORD ordinal array, parallel to names) →
AddressOfFunctions (DWORD RVA array of function pointers, indexed by ordinal). The
resolution algorithm: binary-search AddressOfNames for the target function name, read
the parallel ordinal from AddressOfNameOrdinals, index into AddressOfFunctions with
that ordinal, and add the module base address to get the function's virtual address.
SEC670 Unit 40 tasks students with reimplementing GetProcAddress — the same primitive
T-004 PEB Walker implements by walking gs:[0x60] → PEB → Ldr → InLoadOrderModuleList
to find ntdll, then traversing its export table to resolve Nt* functions. This
traversal is the shared foundation for T-004 (API resolution), T-006 (module stomping,
which must locate export functions to stomp), and T-008 (thread hijacking, which must
resolve function addresses for hijack targets).
clusters.technical_anchor: IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY traversal: AddressOfNames (DWORD* RVA array) → binary search → AddressOfNameOrdinals (WORD* parallel array) → AddressOfFunctions[ordinal] (DWORD RVA) + base address = function VA — reimplemented as custom GetProcAddress via PEB → Ldr → InLoadOrderModuleList
clusters.priority_reason: Two member notes; documents the PE export resolution mechanism shared by three existing cards (T-004, T-006, T-008); foundational prerequisite.

clusters.canonical_name: Network Serialization and Endianness for C2 Protocol Design
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note about byte-order serialization concerns for C2 protocol design, not documented in T-022.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 covers serialization concerns specific to C2 protocol design: byte ordering
(_byteswap_ushort/ulong/uint64 for big-endian to little-endian conversion on x86/x64,
which is natively little-endian), serialization libraries (alpaca, a header-only C++
binary serialization library), and C++20 std::bit_cast for type-safe reinterpretation
of raw bytes between same-size types without violating strict aliasing. The vault's
T-022 documents HTTP transport but does not address the binary protocol layer above it.
A card should document the endianness differential between x86/x64 (little-endian) and
network byte order (big-endian, per RFC 791), the hton*/ntoh* and _byteswap_* families,
the tradeoff between binary (compact, fast, fragile to schema changes) and text (JSON,
verbose, flexible) serialization for C2 protocols, and how the vault's Rust-based
protocol (client_rust crate) handles serialization (likely via serde + bincode or
postcard).
clusters.technical_anchor: _byteswap_ushort/ulong/uint64 (MSVC intrinsics for bswap16/32/64) + C++20 std::bit_cast<To, From>() for type-punned reinterpretation + alpaca header-only serialization library
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents the C2 binary protocol layer (serialization, endianness) that T-022's HTTP transport sits beneath.

clusters.canonical_name: NtSetInformationObject Handle Flag Manipulation (Protect-from-Close)
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note about NtSetInformationObject with ObjectHandleFlagInformation for handle-table entry manipulation, not documented in T-016.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 unit 3 documents the handle table Entry bit fields — Lock, Inheritable, Audit,
and Protect-from-close — and explicitly names NtSetInformationObject with
ObjectHandleFlagInformation (class 0) as the API to manipulate the Protect-from-close
and Inheritable flags. The OBJECT_HANDLE_FLAG_INFORMATION structure contains two
BOOLEAN fields: Inherit (whether the handle is inherited by child processes) and
ProtectFromClose (whether CloseHandle on this handle returns ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE
instead of closing). Setting ProtectFromClose=1 prevents the handle from being closed,
which can be used to pin open handles to resources (e.g., a file handle to a deleted
file, preserving its data) or to prevent EDR from closing handles to monitored
resources. The vault's T-016 (NTAPI Hook Evasion) does not document this handle-
manipulation primitive. A card should document the OBJECT_HANDLE_FLAG_INFORMATION
structure, the NtSetInformationObject call, the detectability (ObjectHandleFlagInformation
is a rare information class), and operational scenarios for Protect-from-close.
clusters.technical_anchor: NtSetInformationObject(ObjectHandleFlagInformation, class 0) with OBJECT_HANDLE_FLAG_INFORMATION {Inherit, ProtectFromClose} — ProtectFromClose=1 makes CloseHandle return ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents a specific NT API for handle-table manipulation with evasion and pinning use cases; named primitive.

clusters.canonical_name: COM Apartment Mode as Hijack Targeting Variable
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note about COM apartment mode (STA vs MTA) as a variable that determines which InprocServer32 entries are viable hijack targets.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 unit 15 frames CoInitialize as a binary prerequisite for COM hijacking, but
the COM apartment mode — STA (Single-Threaded Apartment) via CoInitialize(NULL) or
CoInitializeEx(NULL, COINIT_APARTMENTTHREADED) vs. MTA (Multi-Threaded Apartment) via
CoInitializeEx(NULL, COINIT_MULTITHREADED) — determines which InprocServer32 threading
model entries a host process will load. The registry key
HKCR\CLSID\{CLSID}\InprocServer32 has a ThreadingModel value (Apartment, Free, Both,
or Neutral). A process in STA will only load DLLs with ThreadingModel=Apartment or
Both; a process in MTA will only load ThreadingModel=Free or Both. T-017 (COM Hijack
persistence) does not document apartment-aware targeting. A card should document the
apartment-mode matrix, the CoInitialize/CoInitializeEx flag values, the ThreadingModel
registry values, and how to enumerate viable hijack targets by matching the host
process's apartment mode to the InprocServer32 ThreadingModel.
clusters.technical_anchor: CoInitializeEx(NULL, COINIT_APARTMENTTHREADED) for STA vs CoInitializeEx(NULL, COINIT_MULTITHREADED) for MTA — InprocServer32 ThreadingModel value (Apartment/Free/Both/Neutral) determines loadability
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents a targeting variable that affects COM hijack viability in T-017; operational precision value.

clusters.canonical_name: Multi-Language Tool Diversity as Signature-Attribution Defense
clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note about using multiple programming languages (C, C++, Rust, C#, Go) to prevent signature attribution across operations.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 unit 26 explicitly recommends developing offensive tools across C, C++, Rust,
C#, and Go so that signature attribution cannot tie multiple operations to a single
toolchain. Each language produces distinctive binary characteristics: C/C++ produce
unmanaged native code with MSVC or GCC ABI signatures; Rust produces native code with
unique monomorphized generics and panic-handling patterns; C# produces managed IL
assemblies with CLR metadata; Go produces statically linked binaries with Go runtime
signatures (goroutine scheduling, channel primitives). The vault is currently Rust-only
(dark_crystal, client_rust), meaning all vault-derived tooling shares Rust-attributable
binary features (panic string table, trait vtable layout, proc macro artifacts). A
concept card should document the per-language attribution surface (compiler
signatures, runtime artifacts, import patterns, section names), the rationale for
diversification (preventing cross-operation correlation), and the operational cost
(maintaining multiple toolchains, payload format compatibility across languages).
clusters.technical_anchor: Per-language binary attribution: Rust (panic string table, monomorphized generics, .rustc section) vs Go (goroutine scheduler, runtime signatures) vs C# (CLR metadata, IL disassembly) vs C/C++ (MSVC/GCC ABI signatures)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but articulates a cross-cutting attribution-evasion philosophy relevant to all vault tooling; operational tradecraft value.

custom command parsing and execution). A card should document the three AMSI bypass
approaches (patching, hardware breakpoint, exception-based), the AmsiScanBuffer
function signature and its role in the AMSI pipeline (amsi.dll → AmsiScanBuffer →
AV/EDR scan provider), and the CustomShell alternative as a fourth approach (bypassing
by avoidance rather than by patching).
clusters.technical_anchor: AmsiScanBuffer in amsi.dll — patching approach (prologue overwrite: mov eax, 1; ret) vs HW breakpoint (DR1 via SetThreadContext) vs PAGE_GUARD (VirtualProtect on AmsiScanBuffer memory)
